Q362.L1t: The passage is a first-person account of a teenager describing his pride in looking after his younger siblings.
Q362.L2t: The writer's brother lost the use of the lower two-thirds of his body after being hit by a pick-up truck at nine and has used a wheelchair for six years.
Q362.L3t: The writer says he watches over four sisters and a brother, and that his brother needs more attention than most siblings do.
Q362.L4t: The text shows that a big brother sometimes has to take on extra responsibility, because one sibling needs more care than the others.
Q362.L2f: The writer's brother was hurt in a car accident at the age of twelve and has needed a wheelchair for only a few months.

Q362.L4f: The text shows that a big brother must put up with incredible hardship.

Q367.L1t: The passage is an argument about how people learn vocabulary in their mother tongue compared with a second language.
Q367.L2t: The writer says he picked up about 30,000 words of his mother tongue unconsciously, and that around five percent of the words we think we know are mislearnt.
Q367.L3t: The writer argues that guessing from context produces many wrongly-guessed meanings, and that a good dictionary, which lists the many separate meanings of words, is what makes self-learning possible.
Q367.L4t: The writer's certain conclusion is that learners should look words up in a dictionary and so get the separate meanings of each word, instead of guessing.
Q367.L2f: The writer says that only about one word in a thousand is ever mislearnt by native speakers, and these errors vanish quickly.
Q367.L3f: The writer claims that guessing from context is reliable and almost always gives the right meaning, so dictionaries are rarely needed.
Q367.L4f: The writer's certain conclusion is that the best way to learn new words is to guess their meanings from the context.

Q446.L1t: Courts review the constitutionality of laws using different tiers of scrutiny, depending on the right or classification involved.
Q446.L2t: Voting is treated as a fundamental right under the Constitution, so laws that burden it are not judged under the most deferential standard.
Q446.L3t: When a law burdens a fundamental right, courts apply strict scrutiny, which upholds the law only if it is narrowly tailored and necessary to serve a compelling government interest.
Q446.L4t: If the court upholds the law, the law must be necessary to achieve a compelling government purpose.
Q446.L2f: The Supreme Court first recognised voting as a protected constitutional interest in the early twentieth century, and states have regulated elections ever since.
Q446.L3f: Voting laws are reviewed under a middle-tier test that asks only whether the law is closely connected to a legitimate government aim, with no need for the aim to be important or compelling.
Q446.L4f: If the court upholds the law, the law need only be substantially related to a legitimate government purpose.
